headline: Corona Man Bitten While Using Barbecue Tongs to Remove Rattlesnake
summary: A man in Corona, California was bitten by a rattlesnake while trying to remove it with barbecue tongs, according to a WBRZ report. SnakeNews breaks down the danger and shares essential snakebite safety advice.
body:
I'm Philip Massouh, and this is SnakeNews. Breaking tonight out of Corona, California, where a man has learned a lesson that should be obvious to anyone who's ever watched a nature documentary: barbecue tongs are for flipping burgers, not for wrangling rattlesnakes. The report comes to us from WBRZ, and the headline could not be more SnakeNews if we'd written it ourselves. A man was bitten while using barbecue tongs to remove a rattlesnake. That's the entire story in one sentence, and it's enough to make my dad and uncle start checking under the couch cushions again.

Let me say it again, slowly, for the people in the back. A man. Barbecue tongs. A rattlesnake. A bite. We don't know his name. We don't know his age. We don't know where on his body the snake got him. We don't know if he's recovering in a hospital or if he walked it off. The source report from WBRZ gives us the bare facts, and we are not going to invent a single detail beyond that. But what we can tell you is that this is a perfect example of what not to do, and it's why the SnakeNews Safety Desk exists.

Now let's go to the SnakeNews Safety Desk. I'm joined by our own safety coordinator, Rex Scales. Rex has been with SnakeNews since the great garden hose incident of last summer, and he has one message for anyone who encounters a rattlesnake. Rex, take it away. Rex says, and I quote, 'Call 911 immediately if you're bitten. Stay calm. Keep the bitten limb still and at or below heart level. Do not apply a tourniquet. Do not cut the wound. Do not try to suck out the venom. And for the love of all that is holy, put down the barbecue tongs.' Thank you, Rex. That's advice we can all use, even if we never leave Santa Monica.

Let me break that down for you, because this is important. Calling 911 gets professional medical help on the way. Staying calm slows your heart rate and slows the spread of venom. Keeping the limb still and below heart level also slows venom. A tourniquet can cut off blood flow and cause tissue damage. Cutting the wound can lead to infection and doesn't remove venom. Sucking out venom is a movie myth; it doesn't work and can make things worse. The only thing you should do with your mouth is talk to the 911 dispatcher. And keep the barbecue tongs far, far away.

And if you see a rattlesnake before it bites, give it space. Most bites happen when people try to handle or kill the snake. Call a professional. Keep pets and children inside. Watch from a safe distance. Do not poke it with a stick. Do not throw rocks at it. And absolutely do not grab the barbecue tongs. A cornered snake is a dangerous snake, and a pair of tongs is not a snake hook.

Now, about the animal itself. The source calls it a rattlesnake, and that's all we know for sure. Rattlesnakes are pit vipers, a group of venomous snakes found throughout the Americas. Here in Southern California, and specifically in Riverside County where Corona sits, we have several species, including the Southern Pacific rattlesnake. These snakes are not out to get anyone. They are defensive animals. They strike when they feel cornered, threatened, or when someone waves a pair of metal tongs in their face. They live in chaparral, rocky hillsides, and sometimes in backyards, especially as the weather warms up. They eat rodents. They keep the ecosystem in balance. They deserve our respect, not our barbecue utensils.

Rattlesnakes can be identified by their triangular head, vertical pupils, and of course the rattle at the end of the tail. But not all rattlesnakes rattle before striking. They may stay silent. That's why you should never approach one. In Corona, the most common species is the Southern Pacific rattlesnake, which can be found from the coast into the mountains. They're active mostly in warmer months, but with our changing climate, they can show up almost any time.

And now, the segment my dad and uncle wait for every single day: the Santa Monica check-in. Dad, Uncle, I am fine. I have not seen a single snake today. I have not been bitten. My barbecue tongs are in the kitchen drawer, right next to the spatula, where they belong. The only thing I've removed with tongs this week is a bagel from the toaster, and even that was a little risky. Santa Monica remains, as far as I can tell, snake-free. But the lesson from Corona applies everywhere. If you see a rattlesnake, do not engage. Do not poke it. Do not try to move it. Back away slowly, keep an eye on it, and call animal control or a professional wildlife removal service. Leave the heroics to the professionals. And leave the tongs for the hot dogs.

Dad, I know you're watching. Uncle, I know you're already on the phone with Dad. I'm fine. The closest thing to a snake in my apartment is the cord behind the TV. I checked the patio, I checked the car, I even checked the mailbox. No snakes. But if one does show up, I promise I will not reach for the barbecue tongs. I will back away, call animal control, and then call you both to tell you I'm okay. That's the SnakeNews promise.

For SnakeNews, I'm Philip Massouh. Stay safe, stay calm, and remember: barbecue tongs are not snake handling equipment. This has been SnakeNews.
